info.name: WALLET API
info.description:
API checks for the WALLET service.

Covers all twelve endpoints from spec §5: status codes, response-body schema on every single request, the five token states, the validation boundaries from §4.3, and the malformed-input paths that must produce 400 rather than 500.

Two conventions worth knowing before reading:

1. The environment holds exactly two variables, {{baseUrl}} and {{token}}. Everything else the run needs — ids of rows it created, the second user's token, the expired token — lives in collection variables, set at runtime. There is not one literal id or URL anywhere in the requests.

2. Every response is validated against a JSON Schema, including error responses. Spec §5 says every error has the same shape; a contract nobody asserts is a contract that drifts.

The collection creates its own users on every run, with e-mail addresses derived from a run id, so it is safe to run repeatedly against the same database and in any environment.

exec: // Runs before every request. Sets up two things once per run: the JSON
// Schemas that every response is validated against, and a run id that keeps
// the users this collection creates unique, so it can be run repeatedly
// additionalProperties is false everywhere on purpose: a field that
// appears without anyone deciding to add it is exactly what a contract
// test is for. If the API grows a field, this fails and someone updates
properties: { code: { type: 'string', minLength: 1 }, message: { type: 'string', minLength: 1 } }
properties: { status: { type: 'string' }, version: { type: 'string' }, db: { type: 'string' } }
// null is "no limit set", which is a different state from 0
// ("nothing may be spent"). See qa/docs/analysis-monthly-limit.md A3.
properties: { items: { type: 'array', items: transaction }, total: { type: 'integer', minimum: 0 } }
// May be negative: spending more than you earned is a fact the
// The monthly spending limit and the state it produces
// limit is set; limit_remaining_cents goes negative once exceeded.
// Assertion helpers. Loaded into each test with:
// Keeping them here rather than repeating them in 50 test scripts means the
// schema assertion cannot be quietly forgotten on one request.
"function expectStatus(code) { pm.test('status is ' + code, function () { pm.response.to.have.status(code); }); }",
"function expectSchema(name) { pm.test('body matches the ' + name + ' schema', function () { pm.response.to.have.jsonSchema(schemaFor(name)); }); }",
"    if (errCode) { pm.test('error code is ' + errCode, function () { pm.expect(pm.response.json().error.code).to.eql(errCode); }); }",
"    pm.test('404 and NOT 403 — does not confirm another user\\'s row exists (spec §4.3)', function () {",
"        pm.expect(pm.response.code, 'a 403 here would leak that the row exists').to.not.eql(403);",
"function expectNoBody() { pm.test('204 carries no body', function () { pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.have.lengthOf(0); }); }"

item.name: 403 is unreachable — every cross-user path answered 404

request.description: Spec §5's table lists 403 as 'valid token, but not allowed'. This application has no such case by design: everything a user is not allowed to see answers 404 instead, so that ids cannot be probed for existence (§4.3). Rather than invent an endpoint to produce a 403, this asserts the property that replaced it — the last of the cross-user paths, from the opposite direction.

item.name: 09 · Login rate limiting
item.description:
Spec §5 / D-016: after LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES failed attempts inside LOGIN_WINDOW_MS, login answers 429 with Retry-After until the window expires. The limits come from the runner as globals, so these cases do not hard-code the boundary they are testing.

Two requests here deliberately wait for real time to pass. Everywhere else in this project a fixed wait is forbidden — but a window that expires on a schedule cannot be tested without letting the schedule run, and the alternative (an endpoint that resets the counter) would be test scaffolding shipped in the application.

This folder is last on purpose: it deliberately gets the client IP blocked, and any login after it would inherit that.
